title: Language Barriers and Pain Scales in Emergency Care
summary: Assess pain across languages in emergency care using interpretation, appropriate scales, teach-back, and consistent reassessment.
body_markdown:
###


Yes, self-report remains the preferred approach when the patient can describe pain with appropriate language support. In an emergency department, interpretation should clarify the scale and its anchors without choosing a score for the patient.


###


The clinician should define the endpoints in plain language, and the interpreter should convey the explanation without adding a score. In an emergency department, ask the patient to explain what the endpoints mean before recording the number, then document the scale used.


###


A behavioral pain scale is appropriate when the patient cannot reliably self-report because of age, cognition, consciousness, intubation, or another clinical limitation. A language difference alone is not a reason to replace self-report, because interpretation can support the patient’s own description.


###


Reassess with the same scale and comparable language support whenever clinically appropriate. In an emergency department, follow the organization’s medication and reassessment policy, record the time, score, functional change, adverse effects, and interpretation modality, and investigate an unexpected change rather than assuming translation drift.


###


Yes, a healthcare-specific AI interpreter with appropriate controls may be used as a first-line option for routine pain assessment when organizational policy permits. The emergency team should confirm the patient’s preferred language and dialect, use teach-back, document the modality, and move to a human interpreter according to patient preference, local policy, or encounter needs.
